guide.title: Airway Anatomy & Physiology
guide.lead: Air has to travel from the nose and mouth to the alveoli. In an unresponsive patient the tongue is the usual blocker, and children are built differently. Know where each problem sits and you know which fix to reach for.

sections.title: From nose to alveoli
rows: Shared path for air and food
The tongue falls back here when tone is lost
Narrowest point of the adult airway
Splits into the two mainstem bronchi
The right bronchus is more vertical: objects and deep tubes go right
Gas exchange: O₂ in, CO₂ out

sections.title: Children are not small adults
rows: Large: flexes the neck when supine
Compare with age, not adult norms

steps.title: Head-tilt / chin-lift
steps.text: No suspected spinal injury: lifts the tongue off the back of the pharynx.

steps.title: Jaw thrust
steps.text: Suspected spinal injury: open the airway without moving the neck.

quiz.q: In an unresponsive supine patient, the most common airway obstruction is:
quiz.explanation: With lost muscle tone the tongue falls back against the posterior pharynx.

quiz.q: Gas exchange between the lungs and the blood happens in the:
In a young child, the narrowest part of the airway is the:
quiz.explanation: In adults it is the vocal cords.

quiz.q: Which structure covers the glottis during swallowing?
quiz.explanation: It directs food into the esophagus.

quiz.q: An ET tube advanced too far usually enters the:
quiz.explanation: The right bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical.

quiz.q: Which manoeuvre opens the airway without moving the neck?
quiz.explanation: Use it when a spinal injury is suspected.

quiz.q: How do you keep an infant's airway neutral when lying flat?
options: Flex the chin to the chest
quiz.explanation: The large occiput flexes the neck.
Compare children with their age range.

quiz.q: Why does a small amount of swelling matter more in a child?
options: The airway is narrower, so resistance rises steeply
quiz.explanation: Small changes in radius have a large effect on airflow.

quiz.q: Normal respiratory rate for an infant?

flashcards.question: Commonest airway obstruction (unresponsive, supine)
flashcards.answer: The tongue falling back against the posterior pharynx.

flashcards.question: Epiglottis
flashcards.answer: Covers the glottis during swallowing, keeping food out of the trachea.

flashcards.question: Where is gas exchanged?
flashcards.answer: In the alveoli, across the alveolar-capillary membrane (O₂ in, CO₂ out).

flashcards.question: Why do aspirated objects go right?
flashcards.answer: The right mainstem bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical.

flashcards.question: Narrowest point of the airway
flashcards.answer: Adult: vocal cords. Young child: the cricoid, below the cords.

flashcards.question: Child's tongue
flashcards.answer: Large for the mouth, so it obstructs easily.

flashcards.question: Keeping a small child's airway neutral
flashcards.answer: Pad under the shoulders to offset the large occiput.

flashcards.question: Head-tilt/chin-lift vs jaw thrust
flashcards.answer: Jaw thrust when spinal injury is suspected; otherwise head-tilt/chin-lift.

critical.scenario: An unresponsive adult is supine and snoring loudly with each breath. SpO₂ 90%.
critical.question: Most likely cause and first action?

options.t: The tongue: open the airway with a head-tilt/chin-lift

options.f: Fluid gurgles; snoring is the tongue.

critical.explanation: Then consider an adjunct to keep it open.
critical.kpi: Recognizes tongue obstruction and performs a manual airway maneuver

critical.scenario: A 2-year-old is unresponsive. A new provider puts a folded towel under the child's head, as for an adult.
critical.question: What's the problem?

options.t: It flexes the neck and can block the airway: pad under the shoulders instead

options.f: The large occiput already flexes the neck.

critical.explanation: Neutral position for infants and small children.

critical.scenario: After an intubation, breath sounds are heard only over the right chest.
critical.question: Most likely explanation?

options.t: The tube is in the right mainstem bronchus
options.f: Correct: it's straighter, so deep tubes go right.
Possible, but a deep tube is the commonest cause.
That gives no breath sounds on either side.

critical.explanation: Pull back carefully and reassess; confirm with capnography.
critical.kpi: Recognizes right mainstem intubation from unilateral breath sounds
